final_answer:
merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm. it works by recursively splitting a list into two halves until each sublist has one element (which is trivially sorted). then it merges adjacent sorted sublists into one sorted list.

here’s the step-by-step process:
1) split the list into left and right halves.
2) recursively apply merge sort to the left half until it is sorted.
3) recursively apply merge sort to the right half until it is sorted.
4) merge the two sorted halves into one sorted list by comparing elements from each half and appending the smaller one to a new list.

merge sort runs in o(n log n) time in all cases (best, average, worst), making it predictable.

merge sort is preferred for linked lists over quicksort because of memory access patterns and partitioning challenges:
- quicksort generally relies on random access and partitioning (moving elements around), which is inefficient for linked lists since you can’t easily access the k-th element in o(1) time. linked list operations are sequential, making quicksort’s partitioning expensive.
- merge sort’s merge step naturally works with linked lists. you can merge two sorted linked lists by traversing them and adjusting pointers, which is efficient and avoids the overhead of copying large sections of the list (as you might do with arrays).

in short, merge sort is more cache-efficient and structurally suited for linked lists, while quicksort’s performance degrades on linked lists due to poor locality and expensive partitioning.
